docs.title: AI Infrastructure Engineering
docs.text:
"Wrappers are a commodity. AI Infrastructure is the physics of scale."

This is a living engineering journal tracking hands-on progress through the full AI infrastructure stack — from CUDA memory hierarchies to multi-node serving clusters. Each stage pairs conceptual depth with a concrete practice project and benchmarks.

docs.title: Why This Exists
docs.text:
LLM inference is almost always memory-bound, not compute-bound. Most engineers optimizing AI systems are operating at the wrong level of abstraction — tuning Python when the bottleneck is on-chip bandwidth, or scaling horizontally when the real fix is kernel fusion.

This journal is built on the conviction that you cannot optimize what you don't understand at the silicon level. Each stage builds the mental model and produces a concrete artifact — a profiled kernel, a serving benchmark, a routing proxy — that proves the understanding is real.

Status: 🔄 In Progress

docs.title: What to Learn
docs.text:
• C++ & Rust — systems-level memory management, pointer arithmetic, ownership models
  • CUDA Memory Hierarchy — registers → L1/shared memory → L2 → HBM (global memory)
  • PCIe vs NVLink — bandwidth, latency, topology implications for multi-GPU systems
  • Thread blocks & warp scheduling — SIMT execution model, divergence, occupancy

docs.title: CUDA Memory Hierarchy
docs.text:
Register File       ~10 TB/s    Per-thread, fastest
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Shared Memory / L1  ~20 TB/s    Per-SM, programmer-managed
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L2 Cache            ~10 TB/s    On-chip, shared across SMs
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
HBM (Global DRAM)   ~3.35 TB/s  Off-chip (H100 SXM5)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PCIe (host↔device)  ~64 GB/s    System interconnect
NVLink 4.0          ~900 GB/s   GPU↔GPU (H100)

The Bandwidth Cliff

Moving data from shared memory to global memory is ~6× slower. Moving from GPU to CPU over PCIe is ~50× slower than HBM bandwidth. Most inference bottlenecks trace back to unnecessary memory movement.

docs.title: Warp Scheduling
docs.text:
• A warp is 32 threads executing in lockstep (SIMT)
  • An SM (Streaming Multiprocessor) on H100 has 128 CUDA cores → runs 4 warps simultaneously
  • Occupancy = active warps / maximum warps per SM
  • High occupancy hides memory latency by switching warps while one waits on a memory fetch

docs.title: PCIe vs NVLink
docs.text:
Interconnect Bandwidth (bidirectional) Latency PCIe 5.0 x16 ~128 GB/s ~1–2 µs NVLink 4.0 ~900 GB/s <1 µs NVLink 5.0 (B100) ~1800 GB/s <1 µs

NVLink matters for tensor parallelism — all-reduce operations between GPUs use this fabric.

docs.title: Practice Project: CUDA Matrix Multiplication
docs.text: Goal: Write a CUDA kernel for matrix multiplication from scratch, then profile it against cuBLAS.

docs.title: Naive Kernel
docs.text:
__global__ void matmul_naive(float* A, float* B, float* C,
                              int M, int N, int K) {
    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;

    if (row < M && col < N) {
        float sum = 0.0f;
        for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) {
            sum += A[row * K + k] * B[k * N + col];
        }
        C[row * N + col] = sum;
    }
}

Problem: Each thread reads from global memory K times. For K=4096, that's 4096 uncached global reads per thread. Memory bandwidth is destroyed.

docs.title: Tiled Kernel (Shared Memory)
docs.text:
#define TILE_SIZE 32

__global__ void matmul_tiled(float* A, float* B, float* C,
                              int M, int N, int K) {
    __shared__ float sA[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];
    __shared__ float sB[TILE_SIZE][TILE_SIZE];

    int row = blockIdx.y * TILE_SIZE + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * TILE_SIZE + threadIdx.x;
    float sum = 0.0f;

    for (int t = 0; t < (K + TILE_SIZE - 1) / TILE_SIZE; t++) {
        if (row < M && t * TILE_SIZE + threadIdx.x < K)
            sA[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = A[row * K + t * TILE_SIZE + threadIdx.x];
        else
            sA[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = 0.0f;

        if (col < N && t * TILE_SIZE + threadIdx.y < K)
            sB[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = B[(t * TILE_SIZE + threadIdx.y) * N + col];
        else
            sB[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = 0.0f;

        __syncthreads();

        for (int k = 0; k < TILE_SIZE; k++)
            sum += sA[threadIdx.y][k] * sB[k][threadIdx.x];

        __syncthreads();
    }

    if (row < M && col < N)
        C[row * N + col] = sum;
}

docs.title: Benchmarking Template
docs.text:
import torch
import time

def benchmark(fn, *args, warmup=5, iters=50):
    for _ in range(warmup):
        fn(*args)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(iters):
        fn(*args)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

    return elapsed / iters * 1000  # ms

M, N, K = 4096, 4096, 4096
A = torch.randn(M, K, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)
B = torch.randn(K, N, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)

cublas_time = benchmark(torch.matmul, A, B)
flops = 2 * M * N * K
tflops = flops / (cublas_time / 1000) / 1e12

print(f"cuBLAS: {cublas_time:.2f} ms | {tflops:.1f} TFLOP/s")

docs.title: Stage 2 — Transformer Inference Physics
docs.text:
"LLM inference is almost always memory-bound, not compute-bound."

Status: ⏳ Pending

docs.title: What to Learn
docs.text:
• Prefill vs Decode phases — fundamentally different compute profiles
  • Arithmetic intensity — FLOPs per byte of memory moved (the roofline model)
  • Memory bandwidth bottlenecks — why weights dominate at small batch sizes
  • KV-cache math — memory footprint formula, growth per token

docs.title: The Two Phases of Inference
docs.text:
PREFILL                          DECODE
───────────────────────         ─────────────────────────
Input: full prompt tokens        Input: 1 new token per step
Output: first token + KV cache   Output: 1 token per step

Compute profile: HIGH            Compute profile: LOW
(matrix × matrix, parallel)      (matrix × vector, sequential)

Bound by: COMPUTE                Bound by: MEMORY BANDWIDTH

Why this asymmetry matters

During prefill you're doing a large GEMM (compute-bound). During decode you're loading the entire model weight matrix just to multiply it by a single vector. You use ~1% of your compute capacity and waste 99%. Every optimization for decode is about hiding or reducing memory bandwidth cost.

docs.title: Arithmetic Intensity & the Roofline Model
docs.text:
Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs / bytes of memory traffic

For a 70B parameter model (BF16) at batch_size=1: - Weights: 140 GB - FLOPs per token (decode): ~140 × 10⁹ multiply-adds = 280 GFLOPs - Arithmetic intensity: 280e9 / 140e9 = ~2 FLOPs/byte - H100 ridge point: ~300 FLOPs/byte

Result: 2 << 300 → deeply memory-bound.

docs.title: KV-Cache Memory Math
docs.text:
KV cache size = 2 × num_layers × num_heads × head_dim × seq_len × bytes_per_element

Example (Llama-3 70B, FP16, seq_len=8192):
= 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 8192 × 2 bytes
≈ 42 GB  (!)

docs.title: Memory Bandwidth vs Compute Bound Regimes
docs.text: Batch Size Phase Bottleneck 1 Decode Memory bandwidth (weight loading) 1 Prefill Compute (GEMM) Large (≥32) Decode Can become compute-bound Large Prefill Always compute-bound

docs.title: Practice Project: Profile HuggingFace with Nsight
docs.text:
Goal: Find the exact memory bottleneck during token generation on a real model.

pip install transformers accelerate
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=llm_profile python inference_profile.py

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import nvtx

model_name = "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_name, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map="cuda"
)

prompt = "Explain the attention mechanism in transformers:"
inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")

with nvtx.annotate("PREFILL", color="green"):
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(**inputs, use_cache=True)
        past_kv = outputs.past_key_values

with nvtx.annotate("DECODE", color="red"):
    for step in range(50):
        with nvtx.annotate(f"decode_step_{step}"):
            with torch.no_grad():
                next_token_logits = outputs.logits[:, -1, :]
                next_token = next_token_logits.argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
                outputs = model(
                    input_ids=next_token,
                    past_key_values=past_kv,
                    use_cache=True
                )
                past_kv = outputs.past_key_values

def compute_decode_arithmetic_intensity(model):
    total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
    bytes_moved = total_params * 2
    flops = total_params * 2
    return flops / bytes_moved
# Should be ~1-2, confirming memory-bound operation

docs.title: Stage 3 — Modern Serving Engines & Batching
docs.text:
"Naive batching leaves 60% of GPU VRAM wasted. PagedAttention fixes this."

Status: ⏳ Pending

docs.title: What to Learn
docs.text:
• vLLM — PagedAttention, continuous batching architecture
  • SGLang — RadixAttention, structured generation, prefix caching
  • PagedAttention — paged virtual memory for KV cache
  • Continuous batching — dynamic request scheduling vs static batching
  • Chunked prefill — interleaving prefill chunks with decode steps

docs.title: The Problem with Naive Batching
docs.text:
In static batching, you wait until a batch is full, run it, wait again:

Static Batching:
Time ──►
[req1 ██████████████████████████████████████]  GPU idle waiting
[req2 ██████████████████████████████████████]
[req3 ██████████████████████████████████████]
──────────────────────────────────────────────
                  BATCH RUNS                   New requests queue

Problems: 1. Head-of-line blocking — short requests wait for long ones to finish 2. VRAM fragmentation — each request pre-allocates its maximum sequence length 3. GPU underutilization — GPU idles while batch is being assembled

docs.title: Continuous Batching
docs.text:
Continuous Batching:
Time ──►
[req1  ████ done ]
[req2  ████████████████ done ]
[req3  ██ done ]
[req4           ████ inserted immediately when req1 done ]
[req5                    ████████ inserted when req3 done ]
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        GPU always working — no idle time

docs.title: PagedAttention
docs.text:
Traditional:
[req1: max_len=2048 ████████████████ (actually uses 500 tokens)]
[req2: max_len=2048 ████████████████ (actually uses 200 tokens)]
Wasted: ~60% of allocated VRAM

PagedAttention:
Physical blocks (e.g., 16 tokens each):
[blk0][blk1][blk2][blk3]...[blkN]
Logical pages (per request):
req1 → [blk0][blk3][blk7]           (non-contiguous, grows on demand)
req2 → [blk1][blk5]                  (non-contiguous, grows on demand)
Wasted: ~4% (just last partial page per request)

Why this is transformative

PagedAttention lets you serve 3–4× more concurrent requests on the same GPU by eliminating KV cache fragmentation.

docs.title: Chunked Prefill
docs.text:
Without chunked prefill:
[long prefill: 32K tokens ████████████████████████] decode starved

With chunked prefill (chunk_size = 2048):
[prefill chunk 1 ██][decode][prefill chunk 2 ██][decode]...
TTFT for interactive requests stays low while long context is processed

import asyncio
import aiohttp
import time

async def send_request(session, prompt, max_tokens=100):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    payload = {
        "model": "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        "max_tokens": max_tokens,
        "stream": False
    }
    async with session.post(
        "http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions",
        json=payload
    ) as resp:
        result = await resp.json()
        ttft = time.perf_counter() - start
        return ttft, result

async def load_test(num_requests=50):
    short_prompt = "What is 2+2?"
    long_prompt = "Summarize the history of " + "artificial intelligence " * 200

    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        all_tasks = (
            [send_request(session, short_prompt) for _ in range(num_requests)] +
            [send_request(session, long_prompt, max_tokens=200) for _ in range(5)]
        )
        results = await asyncio.gather(*all_tasks)

    ttfts = [r[0] for r in results]
    print(f"P50 TTFT: {sorted(ttfts)[len(ttfts)//2]*1000:.0f}ms")
    print(f"P99 TTFT: {sorted(ttfts)[int(len(ttfts)*0.99)]*1000:.0f}ms")

asyncio.run(load_test())

docs.title: Stage 4 — KV-Cache & Memory Optimization
docs.text:
"Reused cache is free speed. It can slash Time-To-First-Token by 80%."

Status: ⏳ Pending

docs.title: What to Learn
docs.text:
• Prefix caching — reusing KV blocks for shared prompt prefixes
  • KV quantization — reducing cache precision to INT8/INT4
  • CPU offloading — spilling KV cache to CPU DRAM between requests
  • Multi-turn cache reuse — sharing cache across conversation turns

docs.title: Prefix Caching
docs.text:
Without prefix caching:
Request 1: [system prompt = 500 tok][user query A = 20 tok] → compute all 520 tokens
Request 2: [system prompt = 500 tok][user query B = 20 tok] → compute all 520 tokens again
Cost: 3 × 520 = 1560 token-prefill-compute

With prefix caching:
Request 1: compute 520 tokens, cache KV for first 500
Request 2: cache HIT → compute only 20 new tokens
Cost: 520 + 20 + 20 = 560 token-prefill-compute  (64% reduction)

TTFT reduction

For a 500-token system prompt, prefill takes ~50ms. With a cache hit, TTFT drops to ~5ms. That's an 80–90% TTFT reduction for all requests after the first.

docs.title: Hash-Based Prefix Matching
docs.text:
import hashlib

def compute_block_hash(token_ids: list[int]) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(bytes(token_ids)).hexdigest()

class PrefixCache:
    def __init__(self, block_size=16):
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.cache: dict[str, object] = {}

    def lookup(self, token_ids: list[int]) -> int:
        cached = 0
        for i in range(0, len(token_ids) - self.block_size + 1, self.block_size):
            block = token_ids[i:i + self.block_size]
            h = compute_block_hash(block)
            if h not in self.cache:
                break
            cached += self.block_size
        return cached

docs.title: CPU Offloading
docs.text:
GPU VRAM (80 GB H100):  [Model weights: 70 GB][Hot KV blocks: 10 GB]
                                                          ↕ swap
CPU DRAM (384 GB):      [Cold KV blocks for idle requests: 100+ GB]

Tradeoff: PCIe bandwidth (~64 GB/s) means swapping introduces ~1–5ms latency.

docs.title: Practice Project: KV-Cache Routing Proxy
docs.text:
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
import httpx
import hashlib
from typing import Dict

app = FastAPI()

REPLICAS = [
    "http://replica-a:8000",
    "http://replica-b:8001",
    "http://replica-c:8002",
]

prefix_map: Dict[str, str] = {}

def extract_system_prompt(messages: list) -> str:
    for msg in messages:
        if msg.get("role") == "system":
            return msg.get("content", "")
    return ""

def route_request(system_prompt: str) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256(system_prompt.encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
    if h in prefix_map:
        return prefix_map[h]
    replica = REPLICAS[len(prefix_map) % len(REPLICAS)]
    prefix_map[h] = replica
    return replica

@app.post("/v1/chat/completions")
async def proxy_chat(request: Request):
    body = await request.json()
    system_prompt = extract_system_prompt(body.get("messages", []))
    target = route_request(system_prompt)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=120) as client:
        resp = await client.post(f"{target}/v1/chat/completions", json=body)
    return resp.json()

docs.title: Number Format Comparison
docs.text:
FP32  [sign:1][exp:8][mantissa:23]   Range: ±3.4e38   Precision: ~7 sig digits
FP16  [sign:1][exp:5][mantissa:10]   Range: ±65504    Precision: ~3 sig digits
BF16  [sign:1][exp:8][mantissa:7]    Range: ±3.4e38   Precision: ~2 sig digits
FP8   [sign:1][exp:4][mantissa:3]    Range: ±448      Precision: ~1 sig digit
INT8  [-128 to 127]                   Linear scale      No exponent
INT4  [-8 to 7]                       Linear scale      Very coarse

Why INT4 is tricky

With only 16 representable values, activations with outliers cause large quantization error. AWQ and GPTQ both address this with per-channel or per-group scaling.

docs.title: AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization)
docs.text:
Key insight: not all weights are equally important. Weights that correspond to large activation channels cause outsized quantization error.

from awq import AutoAWQForCausalLM
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

model_path = 'meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct'

model = AutoAWQForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_path)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path)

quant_config = {
    'zero_point': True,
    'q_group_size': 128,
    'w_bit': 4,
    'version': 'GEMM'
}

model.quantize(tokenizer, quant_config=quant_config)
model.save_quantized(quant_path)

docs.title: Practice Project: FP8 vs FP16 Benchmark
docs.text:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from datasets import load_dataset
import time, math

def compute_perplexity(model, tokenizer, max_samples=50) -> float:
    dataset = load_dataset("wikitext", "wikitext-2-raw-v1", split="test")
    encodings = tokenizer("\n\n".join(dataset["text"][:max_samples]), return_tensors="pt")
    max_length, stride, nlls = 2048, 512, []
    for begin_loc in range(0, min(encodings.input_ids.size(1), 8192), stride):
        end_loc = min(begin_loc + max_length, encodings.input_ids.size(1))
        input_ids = encodings.input_ids[:, begin_loc:end_loc].to("cuda")
        target_ids = input_ids.clone()
        target_ids[:, :-1] = -100
        with torch.no_grad():
            outputs = model(input_ids, labels=target_ids)
            nlls.append(outputs.loss.item())
        if end_loc >= encodings.input_ids.size(1):
            break
    return math.exp(sum(nlls) / len(nlls))

def measure_throughput(model, tokenizer, batch_size=1, seq_len=512, num_new_tokens=128):
    dummy_input = torch.randint(0, 32000, (batch_size, seq_len), device="cuda")
    start = time.perf_counter()
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.generate(dummy_input, max_new_tokens=num_new_tokens, do_sample=False)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    return (batch_size * num_new_tokens) / (time.perf_counter() - start)

model_name = "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B"
results = {}

for dtype, torch_dtype in [("fp16", torch.float16), ("bf16", torch.bfloat16)]:
    print(f"\n=== {dtype} ===")
    model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, torch_dtype=torch_dtype, device_map="cuda")
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
    vram = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9
    ppl = compute_perplexity(model, tokenizer)
    tps = measure_throughput(model, tokenizer)
    results[dtype] = {"vram_gb": vram, "perplexity": ppl, "tokens_per_sec": tps}
    print(f"  VRAM: {vram:.1f} GB | PPL: {ppl:.2f} | Throughput: {tps:.0f} tok/s")
    del model
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()

docs.title: Stage 6 — Kernel-Level Engineering
docs.text:
"Python overhead kills inference. Fused kernels save milliseconds that compound at scale."

Status: ⏳ Pending

docs.title: What to Learn
docs.text:
• Triton — Python-based GPU kernel language from OpenAI
  • FlashAttention — memory-efficient attention via tiling
  • CUDA graphs — eliminating CPU launch overhead for repeated workloads
  • Operator fusion — combining multiple ops into a single kernel pass

docs.title: Why Kernel Fusion Matters
docs.text:
Unfused: each op reads/writes to HBM separately
Input → [RMSNorm] → HBM → [Linear] → HBM → [SiLU] → HBM → Output
Total memory traffic: 8 × tensor_size

Fused kernel: intermediates stay in registers/shared memory
Input → [Fused: RMSNorm + Linear + SiLU] → Output
Total memory traffic: 2 × tensor_size
Speedup: 4×+

docs.title: FlashAttention — The Key Idea
docs.text:
Standard attention O(N²) memory:
[Q][K][V] → [S: N×N] → [P: N×N] → [O]  (N² grows fast!)

FlashAttention O(N) memory:
Process Q, K, V in tiles that fit in SRAM.
Never materialize full N×N matrix in HBM.
Result: 2–4× speedup, O(N) memory.

docs.title: Triton Basics
docs.text:
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, output_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(output_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)

import torch
x = torch.randn(1_000_000, device='cuda')
y = torch.randn(1_000_000, device='cuda')
output = torch.empty_like(x)
n = x.numel()
BLOCK_SIZE = 1024
grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK_SIZE),)
add_kernel[grid](x, y, output, n, BLOCK_SIZE)

docs.title: Practice Project: Fused RMSNorm in Triton
docs.text:
import triton
import triton.language as tl
import torch

@triton.jit
def rmsnorm_kernel(
    x_ptr, weight_ptr, output_ptr,
    n_cols, eps,
    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr,
):
    row_idx = tl.program_id(0)
    row_start = row_idx * n_cols
    offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_cols
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + row_start + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    x_sq_mean = tl.sum(x * x, axis=0) / n_cols
    rms = tl.sqrt(x_sq_mean + eps)
    x_norm = x / rms
    weight = tl.load(weight_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=1.0).to(tl.float32)
    tl.store(output_ptr + row_start + offsets, x_norm * weight, mask=mask)

def triton_rmsnorm(x: torch.Tensor, weight: torch.Tensor, eps: float = 1e-6):
    n_rows, n_cols = x.shape
    output = torch.empty_like(x)
    BLOCK_SIZE = triton.next_power_of_2(n_cols)
    rmsnorm_kernel[(n_rows,)](x, weight, output, n_cols, eps, BLOCK_SIZE=BLOCK_SIZE)
    return output

def torch_rmsnorm(x: torch.Tensor, weight: torch.Tensor, eps: float = 1e-6):
    rms = torch.sqrt(x.float().pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + eps)
    return (x.float() / rms * weight.float()).to(x.dtype)

def benchmark(fn, *args, warmup=10, iters=100):
    for _ in range(warmup): fn(*args)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    import time
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(iters): fn(*args)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    return (time.perf_counter() - start) / iters * 1000

N_ROWS, N_COLS = 4096, 4096
x = torch.randn(N_ROWS, N_COLS, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float16)
w = torch.ones(N_COLS, device='cuda', dtype=torch.float16)

assert torch.allclose(torch_rmsnorm(x, w), triton_rmsnorm(x, w), atol=1e-2)

t_torch = benchmark(torch_rmsnorm, x, w)
t_triton = benchmark(triton_rmsnorm, x, w)
print(f"PyTorch: {t_torch:.3f} ms")
print(f"Triton:  {t_triton:.3f} ms")
print(f"Speedup: {t_torch/t_triton:.2f}×")

docs.title: Stage 7 — Distributed Inference & Parallelism
docs.text:
"Single-GPU inference is dead for frontier models. You must master the shard."

Status: ⏳ Pending

docs.title: What to Learn
docs.text:
• Tensor Parallelism (TP) — split individual weight matrices across GPUs
  • Pipeline Parallelism (PP) — split model layers across GPUs
  • Expert Parallelism (EP) — distribute MoE experts across GPUs
  • Communication patterns — AllReduce, AllGather, scatter, pipeline bubbles

docs.title: Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-style)
docs.text:
Column Parallel (split A vertically across N GPUs):
GPU 0: Y₀ = GeLU(X · A₀)   [A₀: d×(4d/N)]
GPU 1: Y₁ = GeLU(X · A₁)   [A₁: d×(4d/N)]
→ AllGather to get full Y

Row Parallel (second linear layer):
GPU 0: Z₀ = Y₀ · B₀
GPU 1: Z₁ = Y₁ · B₁
→ AllReduce Z = Σ Zᵢ

docs.title: Communication Volume for TP
docs.text: At batch=1, seq=2048, hidden=8192 (70B), FP16: - Per AllReduce: 2 × 1 × 2048 × 8192 × 2 = 67 MB - 80 layers × 2 AllReduces = 160 AllReduces per forward pass - At 900 GB/s NVLink: 67 MB / 900 GB/s = 0.07 ms per AllReduce - Total comm overhead: ~11 ms — significant!

docs.title: Pipeline Parallelism
docs.text:
Layers 0–19  → GPU 0
Layers 20–39 → GPU 1
Layers 40–59 → GPU 2
Layers 60–79 → GPU 3

Bubble fraction = (PP_degree - 1) / num_micro_batches

docs.title: Expert Parallelism (MoE)
docs.text:
Token routing: Input → Router → top-K experts selected
GPU 0: Expert 0, 4, 8, ...
GPU 1: Expert 1, 5, 9, ...
→ AlltoAll: gather outputs back to original token positions

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import time

def benchmark_allreduce(tensor_size_mb: float, n_iters: int = 100):
    size = int(tensor_size_mb * 1e6 / 2)  # FP16 = 2 bytes
    tensor = torch.randn(size, device=f'cuda:{dist.get_rank()}', dtype=torch.float16)

    for _ in range(10):
        dist.all_reduce(tensor)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    start = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n_iters):
        dist.all_reduce(tensor)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - start) / n_iters * 1000
    bw = tensor_size_mb * 2 / elapsed * 1000
    return elapsed, bw

if __name__ == "__main__":
    dist.init_process_group("nccl")
    for size in [1, 8, 32, 64, 128, 256]:
        ms, bw = benchmark_allreduce(size)
        if dist.get_rank() == 0:
            print(f"{size:4d} MB AllReduce: {ms:.2f} ms | {bw:.0f} GB/s")

docs.title: Stage 8 — Speculative Decoding
docs.text:
"2× decode speed at zero quality cost is the closest thing to a free lunch in inference."

Status: ⏳ Pending

docs.title: What to Learn
docs.text:
• Draft-target model paradigm — small model proposes, large model verifies
  • Medusa heads — multiple draft heads on the target model itself
  • Acceptance rates — what drives them, how to maximize them
  • N-gram drafting — zero-cost speculation using recent context

docs.title: The Core Insight
docs.text:
Standard decode:
Step 1: run 70B model → 1 token
Step 2: run 70B model → 1 token
...
Cost: N × (70B forward pass)

Speculative decode:
Step 1: run 3B draft × K times → K candidate tokens
         run 70B target ONCE (processes all K tokens in parallel)
         → accept first j tokens where target agrees with draft

If acceptance rate α is high:
  Expected tokens per step = K × α  (e.g., 3 × 0.7 = 2.1 tokens)
  Speedup ≈ 2.1× with identical quality guarantee

docs.title: Acceptance Criterion (Speculative Sampling)
docs.text:
For each proposed token t:
  p = target distribution
  q = draft distribution
  Accept t with probability min(1, p(t)/q(t))
  If rejected: sample from adjusted distribution max(0, p - q)

Output distribution is mathematically identical to the target model.

docs.title: What Determines Acceptance Rate?
docs.text:
• Draft model quality — 7B draft for 70B target works better than 1B
  • Task type — code/structured data → high α (0.7–0.9)
  • Creative generation → lower α (0.4–0.6)
  • Optimal K is typically 4–8

docs.title: N-gram Drafting
docs.text:
from collections import defaultdict

def build_ngram_table(token_ids: list[int], n: int = 3) -> dict:
    table = defaultdict(list)
    for i in range(len(token_ids) - n):
        context = tuple(token_ids[i:i+n])
        table[context].append(token_ids[i+n])
    return table

def ngram_draft(table: dict, context: list[int], n: int = 3, K: int = 5):
    draft, ctx = [], list(context)
    for _ in range(K):
        key = tuple(ctx[-n:])
        if key in table:
            next_tok = table[key][0]
            draft.append(next_tok)
            ctx.append(next_tok)
        else:
            break
    return draft

docs.title: Practice Project: 3B Draft → 70B Target Pipeline
docs.text:
# Using vLLM's built-in speculative decoding
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
    --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct \
    --speculative-model meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct \
    --num-speculative-tokens 5 \
    --speculative-draft-tensor-parallel-size 1 \
    --tensor-parallel-size 4

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import time

# Load models
draft_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda:0"
)
target_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto"
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct")

def speculative_decode(prompt, max_new_tokens=200, K=5, temperature=0.6):
    input_ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda:0")
    generated = input_ids.clone()
    total_tokens, accepted_tokens = 0, 0

    while total_tokens < max_new_tokens:
        with torch.no_grad():
            draft_out = draft_model.generate(
                generated, max_new_tokens=K, do_sample=True,
                temperature=temperature, return_dict_in_generate=True, output_scores=True
            )
        draft_tokens = draft_out.sequences[:, generated.shape[1]:]
        k_actual = draft_tokens.shape[1]

        verify_input = torch.cat([generated, draft_tokens], dim=1).to("cuda")
        with torch.no_grad():
            target_logits = target_model(verify_input).logits
        target_logits_draft = target_logits[:, generated.shape[1]-1:-1, :]

        n_accepted = 0
        for i in range(k_actual):
            p = torch.softmax(target_logits_draft[:, i, :] / temperature, dim=-1)
            q_token = draft_tokens[:, i]
            if torch.rand(1).item() < min(1.0, (p[0, q_token] / 1e-8).item()):
                n_accepted += 1
            else:
                break

        accepted = draft_tokens[:, :n_accepted]
        bonus_pos = generated.shape[1] + n_accepted - 1
        bonus_logits = target_logits[:, bonus_pos, :] / temperature
        bonus_token = torch.multinomial(torch.softmax(bonus_logits, dim=-1), 1)
        generated = torch.cat([generated, accepted.to(generated.device),
                               bonus_token.to(generated.device)], dim=1)
        accepted_tokens += n_accepted
        total_tokens += n_accepted + 1

        if tokenizer.eos_token_id in generated[0, -k_actual:].tolist():
            break

    text = tokenizer.decode(generated[0, input_ids.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)
    return text, accepted_tokens / max(total_tokens, 1)

prompt = "Explain the transformer attention mechanism in detail:"
for K in [1, 3, 5, 7, 10]:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    text, alpha = speculative_decode(prompt, max_new_tokens=100, K=K)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f"K={K}: α={alpha:.2f} | {100/elapsed:.1f} tok/s")
